concerns.text: FR-002 mandates: 'The system MUST NOT impute, interpolate, synthesize, simulate, placeholder, or hardcode any metric values.' In a systematic review of heterogeneous literature, studies frequently report metrics in incompatible units or omit variance (SD/SE) entirely. A strict prohibition on imputation/simulation combined with a requirement to perform meta-analysis (FR-004) creates a logical impossibility: if >50% of studies lack variance, the system must fall back to descriptive stats (FR-004), but if the *raw values* themselves are missing or non-comparable (e.g., 'seconds' vs 'FLOPs' without a baseline), the system cannot compute *any* aggregate metric without imputation or exclusion. The spec fails to define a scientifically valid protocol for handling non-comparable units that are not simply 'missing' but 'incommensurate' without a transformation that might be considered 'synthesis'.

FR-008 defines a 'valid baseline' as 'a reported non-private execution on the same hardware architecture.' FR-009 triggers a sensitivity analysis if >20% of studies lack this. This design introduces a severe selection bias (survivorship bias) that invalidates the meta-analysis. In privacy-preserving FL literature, 'same hardware' baselines are rare; most papers report relative overhead or use different hardware. By excluding >20% of the corpus (likely the majority) from the primary analysis, the resulting 'effect size' is not a measure of the privacy mechanism's cost, but a measure of the cost *only in studies that happened to use identical hardware*. The validation target (the effect size) is thus circularly dependent on a selection criterion (hardware match) that is not a property of the mechanism itself, rendering the scientific claim unsound.

FR-006 mandates using the Kruskal-Wallis H test on 'raw extracted metric values' for group comparison. However, the 'raw values' for 'Computational Cost' are explicitly heterogeneous (seconds, FLOPs, relative ratios) per FR-008 and the Assumptions section. Kruskal-Wallis assumes a common ordinal scale across groups. Comparing 'seconds' from Study A against 'FLOPs' from Study B in a single rank-order test is a category error. The spec requires a statistical test that is mathematically invalid for the data type defined in the same document. The methodology must be revised to either normalize all values to a dimensionless ratio *before* testing (which conflicts with FR-002's anti-synthesis stance) or restrict the test to only the subset of studies with a common unit, acknowledging the reduced power.
